opus-5.5.text:
I think robotics is a natural outlet for world models because it's one of the few places where you can't cheat. With language models, much of the intelligence lives in the space of text: you predict the next token, and the world only shows up indirectly. A robot has to deal with physics, contact, occlusion, objects behaving in ways you didn't anticipate. If your internal model of the world is wrong, the cup falls off the table. That feedback is very honest.

A world model, as I see it, is a system that understands how the world works and can predict what happens next, especially what happens when *you* act. That's exactly what a robot needs. Before reaching for something, it should be able to imagine, roughly, "if I push here, this will slide; if I grasp there, it will tip." That kind of mental simulation is what humans and animals do all the time, and it's what's mostly missing from current robot learning pipelines, which still lean heavily on imitation of collected demonstrations.

There's also a data argument. Robotics has a severe data problem. You can't scrape the internet for robot trajectories the way you scrape text. But there's a huge amount of video of the physical world: people cooking, objects moving, hands manipulating things. A good world model could learn the structure of the physical world from that visual data, and then a robot could build on that foundation instead of learning everything from scratch through expensive teleoperation. So the world model becomes a bridge between abundant passive observation and scarce embodied experience.

And honestly, I think it goes both ways. Robotics needs world models, but world models also need robotics. If we only evaluate world models by how pretty the generated video looks, we may fool ourselves. A video can look plausible and still be physically wrong. Putting the model in the loop with a real agent that has to act and succeed or fail is a much better test of whether it truly understands anything. So for me, robotics is less an "application" and more a proving ground, a place where the question of whether we've built real spatial and physical intelligence finally gets answered.

r001.rationale: The response describes robotics as an application and proving ground for world models, but does not prioritize capable household robots over AGI or superintelligence.

r002.rationale: It gives no benchmark based on a twelve-year-old child's ability to perform household chores.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's because robotics is where the gaps in current vision systems become impossible to ignore. In language, you can get very far with next-token prediction because the data already encodes a lot of human reasoning. But a robot has to act in a physical world, and that world doesn't come pre-tokenized. It has to understand space, how objects persist, what happens if it pushes something, how a scene will look from a different angle a second later. That's exactly what a world model is supposed to provide: an internal representation that can predict how the environment evolves, not just label what's in a frame.

The other reason is that robotics gives you a clear signal about whether the model actually understands anything. With image or video generation, you can be fooled. A clip can look beautiful and still have physics that make no sense, and people will still say "wow." A robot can't be fooled that way. If the model's prediction about the world is wrong, the arm misses the cup, or the cup falls over. That kind of grounded feedback is very valuable for research. It forces us to care about things like 3D consistency, object permanence, and causality, instead of just visual plausibility.

And honestly, robotics is also where the data problem is most interesting. We don't have an internet-scale corpus of robot experience the way we have text. So you can't just scale up imitation. You need a model that can learn general structure about the world from passive video and perception, and then transfer that to a specific embodiment with relatively little interaction data. That's the promise of a world model: learn once about how the world works, then reuse it across tasks and bodies. I don't think we're there yet, and I'd be careful about the hype. But if you ask me where world models will prove their worth first, it's probably not entertainment, it's agents that have to move through and change the physical world.

astra-6.text:
I think robotics gives world models a very concrete purpose. A robot needs to understand not just what it’s looking at, but what will happen if it takes an action. If I push this object, where will it move? If I pick it up this way, will it slip? Those are questions about how the world works, and the answers matter directly for behavior.

You can think of a world model as a way for the robot to anticipate consequences before acting. Instead of learning everything through physical trial and error, it could use that model to compare possible actions and decide which ones are promising. Of course, that only helps if the predictions capture the things that actually matter for the task. Generating something that looks plausible isn’t necessarily enough.

That’s why I find robotics such a compelling outlet: it closes the loop between perception, prediction, and action. The robot acts, observes what really happened, and gets feedback on where its understanding was wrong. You have a concrete test of whether the model’s understanding is useful: does it help the robot accomplish something in the physical world?

sol-6.1.text:
I think robotics gives world models a very concrete purpose. A robot needs to understand not just what it’s looking at, but what might happen when it takes an action. If I push this object, where will it move? If I pick it up this way, will it slip? Those are questions about how the world works, and the answers matter directly for deciding what to do.

The exciting part is the feedback loop. You make a prediction, take an action, and observe the result. So you have a way to test whether the model’s understanding is actually useful. Generating a plausible future is one thing; generating a future accurate enough to guide an action is a much stronger requirement.

That’s why I see robotics as a natural outlet. It connects learning a model of the world with using that model to accomplish something.
